title: Miniature Drum with Four Frogs

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Samuel Eilenberg Collection, Bequest of Samuel Eilenberg, 1998
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A very small bronze drum with a flat circular top and a flared body. Four small frog figures are part of the design.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record (title, date, medium, culture, classification, tags Drums and Frogs, public-domain flag, image URLs, credit line) and the Met catalog page label text

context: A miniature bronze drum from northern Vietnam, made by the Dongson culture between about 500 BCE and 300 CE. It is only about 10 cm tall, and its title says it has four frogs. The Met's label says drums are the most widely spread products of the Dongson culture, and that their function, often as burial finds, is unclear.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny drum made of metal. It has four frogs on it. It is very, very old, more than 1,700 years. Can you find all four frogs?
descriptions.g12: This drum is made of bronze and is very small, only about as tall as a cup. Four frogs are part of its design. People in Vietnam made it more than 1,700 years ago, and maybe much earlier. Why do you think the maker added frogs? What could they mean?
descriptions.g35: This tiny bronze drum comes from the Dongson culture of northern Vietnam. Big Dongson drums were traded far and wide, and this one is a miniature, only about 10 centimeters tall. Four frogs decorate it. Scholars are not sure exactly how these drums were used, though many were found in burials. What can you guess from the frogs and the shape?
descriptions.g68: Dongson drums are among the most widely spread objects made by the culture of northern Vietnam, and this miniature, about 10 cm tall, copies the form on a tiny scale. Four frogs are part of the design, an animal often linked by scholars with rain and water, although the Met does not state a meaning. The label notes that the function of such drums, often found in burials, remains unclear. How can a small copy of a big object still feel important?
descriptions.g910: This miniature bronze drum belongs to the Dongson culture, whose drums were widely distributed across Southeast Asia. Its title notes four frogs, a motif frequently discussed in connection with water and rain, though the Met's label stops short of explaining it and says the function of these drums, often found in burials, remains unclear. At only about 10 cm, the piece raises questions about scale, symbolism, and use. What can an object teach us when its purpose is uncertain?
descriptions.g1112: The Dongson drum tradition is central to the archaeology of early Southeast Asia, and this miniature version raises questions about copying, scale, and meaning. The title tells us it carries four frogs, a motif that scholars often connect with rain and fertility, but the Met's label says the function of such drums, frequently found in burials, remains unclear. A small drum might have served as a model, an offering, or an object of status. Consider what evidence could distinguish these possibilities and how interpretation can proceed responsibly without it.

g1112.emotion: How does a small, finely made object produce a sense of weight and ritual, and is that effect due to the object or to our expectations?
g1112.observation: Describe the drum's formal organization with precision. Where does description start to presume use or meaning?

g1112.texture: In what ways can surface evidence suggest production methods, and what is lost to time?
g1112.space: How does scale shape possible interpretations of the drum as a model, offering, or status object?
g1112.light: How might the object's metallic surface have mattered in ritual or burial settings, and what can we know about that?
g1112.meaning: Evaluate the frequently proposed link between frogs, rain, and fertility. What evidence supports it, and what limits it?
g1112.culture: What does the wide distribution of Dongson drums suggest about networks of exchange, and how should we avoid retrofitting modern national boundaries onto them?

g1112.critical: What standards should govern interpretation of ancient objects found without written explanations?

safety.method: Title, classification (Metalwork), medium (Bronze), culture, and tags (Drums, Frogs) checked against the museum record, and the Met label text on Dongson drums was read. No people or sensitive subject is indicated. The exact placement of the frogs was not described by the record, so descriptions avoid claims about it. The image file itself was not visually inspected in this build. A person should confirm it in the review tool before release.

teacherNote.context: A miniature bronze drum from northern Vietnam, Dongson culture, ca. 500 BCE-300 CE, about 10 cm tall, with four frogs. The Met says its function remains unclear.
directions: Ask students to act as archaeologists: list questions they would ask about a found object whose use is unknown.
Discuss why animals appear as motifs in many cultures and what they might mean.
Have students make a clay miniature of a familiar object and explain what they changed by shrinking it.
